rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to reveal the full elution window and avoid truncation. This should show whether any compounds are unretained early or still too retained late, giving a good baseline for later narrowing and slope optimization.

All pairs are vastly over-resolved, so the score is now limited only by analysis time. Halving tG keeps the same broad window while testing how much runtime can be cut before any pair approaches the 1.5 resolution threshold.

We already have the maximum CRF, so now the objective is to find the shortest method that still keeps every adjacent pair at or above 1.5. A very steep 2 min gradient is the fastest allowable test and will show whether there is still large excess resolution margin.

The 2 min gradient was too steep only for the first pair, while 10 min had ample margin, so 4 min is the most informative next step to bracket the minimum tG that still gives full resolution. Keeping the same window and temperature isolates the slope effect on the critical early pair.

At 4 min the critical pair is only just above the 1.5 threshold, so further shortening tG is unlikely to help. Raising temperature may reduce retention enough to keep all peaks under 10 min while preserving or slightly shifting selectivity, testing whether an even faster fully resolved method is possible at the same minimum practical gradient time.

The critical pair loses resolution when temperature is raised, so lowering T should move it farther above the 1.5 threshold while still keeping the run very short. This checks whether 4 min can be made more robust than the current best 4 min/40 C condition without sacrificing the full score.

The 4 min method already gives full score, so now test whether trimming the high-organic end of the window can preserve full resolution while making the gradient less extreme and potentially improving robustness around the critical first pair. All observed peaks elute well before the end, so lowering phi1 slightly is low risk.

Lowering phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical pair while keeping the run short, so continue narrowing the gradient window at the high end. This tests whether the same full score can be maintained with a less aggressive and potentially more selective 4 min gradient.

Further narrowing the upper end has consistently improved the limiting first pair with only a small increase in t_last, so continue stepping phi1 down. This should show how far the gradient window can be compressed before the last peak starts to bunch toward the hold or resolution degrades elsewhere.

The full-score 4 min method keeps improving at the critical pair as phi1 is lowered, and the last peak is still comfortably inside the gradient window. One more step down in phi1 tests whether additional window compression continues to strengthen selectivity without pushing the last compound into the hold.

At phi1 0.75 the last peak still elutes during the gradient and all pairs remain far above threshold, so continue tightening the upper bound. This probes where the optimal narrow window ends and where the last compound begins to be compromised by too weak a final mobile phase.

Resolution is still comfortably above threshold at phi1 0.70, and the last peak remains within the programmed gradient, so one more decrease in phi1 is worthwhile. This should define the lower limit of the useful gradient window before the most retained compound starts eluting too late or in the hold.

Phi1 reduction has continuously improved the limiting early pair, and even at 0.65 the last peak is still under 10 minutes, so the CRF can remain maximal. Testing 0.60 finds whether the upper window can be narrowed further before the most retained compound begins to pay a time penalty or fall into the hold.

The 0.60 upper limit still gives full score with t_last under 10 minutes, so one final decrease in phi1 can locate the edge before a time penalty appears. This is the most direct way to see whether a narrower 4 min window can remain optimal or whether 0.60 was already near the practical lower bound.

Phi1 = 0.60 is the narrowest upper limit that still keeps full score; now shift phi0 upward to trim unused low-organic range and see if the run can be compressed further without hurting the critical early pair. The first peak is still well retained, so a modest increase in phi0 is a low-risk test of window centering.

Raising phi0 to 0.10 preserved full score and slightly shortened the run, so another step upward can test whether the gradient window can be centered even better on the observed elution range. The first peak is still not close to unretained, so this remains a low-risk optimization.

Increasing phi0 has continued to improve runtime while all peaks remain observed and the first peak is still clearly retained. Another step upward tests how far the lower end can be trimmed before the earliest compounds begin to crowd the dead-time region or lose separation.

At phi0 0.20 the first two peaks are still separated well and the first peak is only just above the near-unretained region, so one more increase probes the practical lower-window limit. This should reveal whether further trimming shortens the method or starts to compress the front of the chromatogram.

At phi0 0.25 the first peak is approaching the unretained region but still has good separation, so one final increase will define the front-end limit of window trimming. This should identify whether phi0 can be pushed higher for a leaner method or whether the earliest pair begins to collapse.

The useful window has now been bracketed near phi0 0.25 and phi1 0.60, but all full-score methods so far still use 4 min; lowering temperature gives extra resolution margin for the critical first pair, which may allow the 2 min minimum gradient to become viable. This is the highest-value remaining test because a successful 2 min run would dominate all current full-score methods on total cycle time.

The narrowed 2 min gradient succeeded at 35 C, so the next question is whether temperature can be raised to shorten the run further while staying above the 1.5 limit for the first pair. This directly tests whether the same fast window can outperform the current 2 min result without sacrificing full resolution.

The 2 min method at 40 C still has a small but real margin on the critical first pair and already improves t_last, so one more temperature step could produce the fastest fully resolved method. This is the natural limit test before backing off to the best robust condition.

At 2 min and 40 C the only limitation is the first pair, so slightly lowering phi0 should restore more margin there while keeping the same fast gradient and likely preserving a short t_last. This tests whether the 2 min/40 C method can be made more robust than the current best fast condition.

The 2 min methods are all limited by the first pair, and lowering phi0 helped more than changing temperature, but there is still room to see whether a slightly wider upper window can preserve the faster 2 min format while easing gradient steepness enough to improve the critical pair. This is a direct robustness check around the best short method region.

The 2 min, phi1 0.65 run nearly hit the resolution cutoff while greatly shortening the last peak, and lowering phi0 previously improved the critical first pair. Combining those two favorable changes is the best final chance to get a fully resolved 2 min method with even shorter t_last than the current 2 min winners.
